So I've taken a huge break in VTES, but it continues to amuse me...
however, there are a few things that keep me from jumping right back
in full force (or even casualy dipping my foot in the waters).

One biggy that I wish to address here is that

Once you sit down at a table, you are contractually obligated to stay
there.

The rules to the game do not allow for standing up from the table and
quitting in a fair manner.

Are there any solutions?

> Once you sit down at a table, you are contractually obligated to stay

No, but depending on the situation, there are certainly consequences
to standing up.

If you are playing in a casual game (i.e. with friends or with random
people in a store) and you get up and leave for no good reason (i.e.
you get cranky and scoop your cards; I'm not really addressing "my
wife called and I need to go pick her up right now" or "Uh oh, my
basement just flooded", as those are both unintentional and
understandable, and everyone will just deal), people will eventually
stop inviting you to play with them, or generally avoid you. As that
is both bad sportsmanship, and kind of dicky.

If you are in a competitive game, if you get up and leave for no good
reason, you are breaking the tournament rules of "not playing to win",
which can get you thrown out of the tournament or banned from future
tournaments (i.e. if you piss off the judge enough, it will eventually
come back to you). And will also result in people not inviting you to
play in the future, presumably, if you make a habit of it. Again, if
your basement floods and you need to get out right then, everyone can
deal. But if you are just cranky and scoop? Not cool.

> The rules to the game do not allow for standing up from the table and
> quitting in a fair manner.

Well, they do, actually--in casual play, people can deal with it
however is appropriate (start over, represent you with some pool
counters, whatever). In tournament play, the Judge can take whatever
action is most appropriate to remedy the situation (rewind the game,
leave a place keeper pool pile, sit in and keep the game going if a
possibility, whatever). I mean, there aren't iron clad rules for
dealing with someone standing up and leaving, but there are plenty of
ways to generally deal with it when it occurs, many of which don't
ruin the current game.

-Peter

Messages.Author: witness1
Messages.Body:
On Jul 10, 1:34 pm, Screaming Vermillian <alexandernja...@gmail.com>
wrote:

> But if there was some formalized system of fairly standing up from the
> table, so that if i DO have to go get my wife or something, I can not
> feel guilty about it.

When possible, leave your deck and/or pool at the table, and come back
for them when the crisis is resolved. The "best" solution is to allow
another player to play your deck for the remainder of the current
game, and have the judge remove you from the tournament at the end of
the round (assuming tournament play).

If you have to take your cards with you for whatever reason (or a
substitute player cannot be found), it can be more difficult for a
judge to handle the situation. However, this is what judges are for,
and there's no particularly good reason to feel guilty about it
(unless, again, you knew in advance that it could be a problem and
decided not to tell anyone).

-witness1

> Which is completely subjective.  What is small, what is large?

Let the predator decide. Pretend the poolsack will successfully
withdraw each turn if nobody at the table takes an action to stop it.

If it's "small" based on where the predator subjectively draws the
line, the predator will take the actions to bleed it out, gain his 6
pool, and earn a VP. The table will be back to something resembling
normality in a few turns at most.

If it's "large" based on where the predator subjectively draws the
line, the predator will allow it to withdraw. The game will be back to
something resembling normality immediately after that happens.

> > If the poolsack is large, you can pretend that the poolsack has traded
> > his deck in for one of those found in this thread:http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/browse_t...
>
> > Let the predator of the poolsack decide whether or not to let the
> > poolsack withdraw each turn.
>
> > For casual games, I would take this to be "fair enough".
>
> What do you think of the "titanium rules"?

I dislike the idea of a player spontaneously gaining up to 5 pool and
up to 1 VP without taking an additional action to acquire it. I
especially dislike the possibility (however remote) of a player with 2
pool and no minions suddenly gaining 5 pool and a VP that, were the
game to have played out "normally", would very likely have instead
been 6 pool and a VP for someone else at the table. In general, I
think players should get no pool nor VPs if they do not manage to
remove their prey's last pool before being ousted themselves.

The spirit of VtES is that getting halfway there and stalling out
rewards your predator, not you.

That doesn't make your idea bad or even unfair. I suspect there are a
lot of situations in which it would work just fine, and I am mostly
focusing on the ones where it doesn't to explain why I don't like it
as a general rule.

I prefer the guidelines I listed above (call them "stainless steel
guidelines"?) because they (mostly) stay within the normal parameters
of how one earns (or fails to earn) VPs.

-witness1

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

On Jul 10, 1:34 pm, Screaming Vermillian <alexandernja...@gmail.com>
wrote:

> But if there was some formalized system of fairly standing up from the
> table, so that if i DO have to go get my wife or something, I can not

No, there isn't, as there are simply too many variables to address--if
it is early in the game, you can just restart; if it is late in the
game, you can just say "I am represented by the number 8..." or
whatever. If you are playing casually, and you need to leave on the
fly (wife calls; you look at your watch and say "holy crap! I gotta go
to work!" or whatever), I'd expect that everyone you are playing would
just adjust as necessary--assuming that you are leaving 'cause you
have no choice and aren't a dick about it, and you are playing
casually, I'd figure that everyone would just adjust as needed, and
either finish out the game as they are capable of, or just throw it in
and start over, with no hard feelings.

VTES is a multi-player game, and one of the flaws of a multi player
game is that if someone has to leave in the middle? It falls apart.
Which is the same with all multi player games, for the most part
(well, except for Titan. Which has rules that specifically say "at the
start of your turn, you can self destruct and remove all of your units
from the map"...)

-Peter

On Jul 10, 9:33 pm, XZealot <xzea...@cox.net> wrote:
> Well, why can't it be an option?

The same reason it can't be an option in Advanced Civ or Axis and
Allies or Diplomacy. 'Cause that is how multi-player games work. It is
a flaw. But trying to make hard and fast rules that address every
possible contingency that comes up when someone just ups and leaves in
the middle isn't a realistic goal. So you just work with what you got
and move on.

> If I have 12 pool, and I want to leave.  Just leaving a poolsack on
> the table royally screws people, but self-ousting also royally screws
> people.  Why can't I just quit and not be hated for doing so?  Why
> can't I quit and why can't I get some rules to ease the pain of
> quitting?

'Cause there are simply too many variables to make rules like this
work well. You can certainly make rules that attempt to cover the
variables, but most of the time, those rules aren't going to be any
better than just figuring out how to fix the issue when it comes up
and dealing with that you have.

> "I'm a newbie and I'm not having fun anymore.  Why can't I quit?"

You can. And we non newbies can say "Well, sorry you didn't have a
good time, maybe we can get you to try again on a later date" and then
pick up the game and start a new one.

Like, whenever this discussion comes up, I'm always totally at a loss
as to why folks aren't just willing to start over a game in the small
number of instances when this sort of thing happens (assuming casual
play; tournament play is a whole other ball of wax, but I'd figure
that you aren't going to likely run into a newbie that is just going
to up and leave in the middle of a game in a tournament). You are
teaching a new guy to play, he stops having a good time, he wants to
go? Ok then. You thank him for playing, and start a new game. How
often is this going to happen that there need to be complicated rules
to address the situation?

I realize that when you (this being the generic "you") are playing a
game, you like to see the outcome. Even if someone ups and leaves in
the middle. But VTES isn't really a game that handles this well, and I
don't think there are any hard and fast rules than can fix that. So
when it happens, you just go on as best you can. And a lot of the time
"going on as best you can" is just going to mean picking up and
starting over. Which isn't optimal, no. But a solution. Why is this
such a bad thing?

-Peter

He gets TWO VPs if he can oust his one prey and deal at least one pool
damage on the poolsack every turn (including the current turn), and
survive until the poolsack is ousted.

If the poolsack is "small" (for varying values of small based on the
decks at the table) he will get the same TWO VPs he was very likely to
have gotten anyway, by ousting two consecutive preys.

If the poolsack is "large" (for varying values of large based on the
decks at the table) he will be unable to earn both VPs before
succumbing himself. If he recognizes this fact far enough in advance,
he can allow the poolsack to withdraw to give him more chances

There is a lot of posts and I didn't go through all of them, but I
figured I could put in my two cents for this piece Vermillian.

For the 'being forced to sit there and die when you know its a lost
cause' aspect. If you feel that you have no chance to win, you may
choose lose your VP in any way that you choose. However, for

"What is the problem with picking up your crap and giving your pred 6

pool and a VP? " - This goes against the rules, because there is no
rule that says you can do that. But if you really feel that you have
no chance you can tell the table that you will block nothing and you
will transfer maximum every turn. Abstain from all voting and no
discard. [You don't even don't have to sit at table and you can go
save wife or dog or hampster or whatever.]

This means that you are not ousted immediately but now everyone knows
that you will be ousted soon. This allows the others to adjust their
gameplay for the eventually player (i.e. you) leaving the table.

Hope this helps.

witness1 wrote:

> He gets TWO VPs if he can oust his one prey and deal at least one pool
> damage on the poolsack every turn (including the current turn), and
> survive until the poolsack is ousted.

> If the poolsack is "small" (for varying values of small based on the

> have gotten anyway, by ousting two consecutive preys.
>
> If the poolsack is "large" (for varying values of large based on the
> decks at the table) he will be unable to earn both VPs before
> succumbing himself. If he recognizes this fact far enough in advance,
> he can allow the poolsack to withdraw to give him more chances

i think we're getting to something workable here with the 'let them
withraw, or not' aspect.

but in the case where perhaps you were relying on their cards to help
you (anarch revolt, dragon bound, fame, etc.), i'd probably go for
something more like this, a "poolsack and a little bit more" approach:

When a player wants to bail:

- their crypt, uncontrolled region, library and hand are removed from
the game. All other cards and counters remain (proxied if necessary if
the player wants to run off with their cards).

- the player is assumed to use no optional effects (tapping cards,
non-compulsory acting, blocking, using MPAs for in-play effects, hunting
grounds, etc).

- apply all mandatory effects as usual (anarch revolt, forced hunts,
etc). These should never require the bailling player's input, working
under the 2nd point, and can be performed by the other players at the
table without bias in general. For the corner case situations where
there are options on a compulsory thing (eg, a ravnos forced hunt under
a Week of Nightmares), randomise among all the possible choices.

- the player is assumed to attempt to withdraw every turn.

- they forfeit all their vps, including any gained from a possible
withdrawal.

This gives options for the predator to make the value judgement as
proposed by witness1 - let them withdraw if it's too much work to get
through, or try and oust them themselves if it looks doable.
But it also gives the prey the opportunity to try and keep their bailled
predator in the game by attacking their vampires, doing pool damage
(krc, kindred spirits, etc) to foil the withdraw attempt. However, these
things will generally work towards ousting the bailled player, so it
would be a fine line to walk.

Thoughts?

I went through a similar phase a while back (when I realized I was
playing more on tournaments than in casual because games sometimes
felt like a real eternal struggle). My solution:

1. Don't just stand up from the table because you feel you've had
enough of that particular game. It is very disrespectful to the
other players. Emergencies, et al, are a different topic of course.

2. If you have less than 2 hours to play, you might be better off to
find something else to do (e.g. just watch the game or something).

3. Play timed games. It only takes as much as agreeing on the 2-hour
limit before the game. Then you know it will not take more than 2
hours - no stalemate lockdown versus wall or rush for example that
can otherwise lead to very long games.

4. If you feel you had enough of the game and really don't have a
reasonable chance to win, go suicide. Just blast into your prey or
whoever locked down your game and die in the process. I often take
pride in taking down wall preys with me (weakening them to the
point that if I don't manage to oust them, my predator will). If
you get lucky, you get VPs, maybe even GW, by being reckless. If
not, then worst comes to worst, you can stand up and move on.

--
Regards,

Daneel
